cards.title: The yield curve: the bond market's recession alarm
cards.body:
The yield curve plots government bond yields across maturities. Normally it slopes upward: lenders demand more to lock money up for ten years than for three months. When short-term yields rise above long-term yields, the curve inverts.

In the U.S., inversion has preceded every recession since the late 1960s, with a lag ranging from roughly six months to two years. The logic: the central bank has pushed short rates up to fight inflation, while long rates fall because markets expect slower growth and future rate cuts. Tight money also squeezes bank lending margins, so credit dries up.

It isn't infallible. The 2022 to 2024 U.S. inversion was the longest on record, and its meaning was hotly debated. Treat it as a shift in probabilities, not a countdown clock.
cards.example: The 10-year yield is 3.5% and the 2-year is 4.2%, so the 10s-2s spread is −0.7 percentage points: inverted. Analysts watch both the 10-year minus 2-year and 10-year minus 3-month spreads, and Canada's curve can be read the same way.
cards.takeaway: An inverted curve says markets expect lower rates and slower growth ahead.

cards.title: The long run: your weekly cornerstone
cards.body:
If you only do one structured session a week, make it the long run. Running continuously for longer than usual drives the adaptations that matter for everything from a 10K to a marathon: more capillaries and mitochondria, larger glycogen stores, tougher tendons, and the mental habit of staying relaxed when tired.

Keep it at an easy, conversational pace, especially at first. A common guideline is that the long run makes up roughly 20 to 30 percent of your weekly distance. Build it gradually, adding one to two kilometres every week or two, with an easier week every third or fourth week.

For runs over about 75 to 90 minutes, practise fuelling: take in carbohydrates during the run, starting around 45 minutes in.
cards.example: Running 30 km a week? Make your long run about 8 to 9 km. Next week try 10 km, then hold there for a week before adding more. A Sunday morning slot works well for most schedules.
cards.takeaway: One easy, gradually longer run a week builds the deepest endurance.

cards.title: Sheet-Pan Paneer Tikka with Chickpeas
cards.body:
Restaurant flavour, one pan, almost no cleanup. Cube a 350 g block of paneer and toss it with a drained can of chickpeas, a sliced red onion and two bell peppers cut into chunks.

For the marinade, mix 1/2 cup Greek yogurt with 1 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp each of cumin, smoked paprika and turmeric, 2 grated garlic cloves, a thumb of grated ginger, salt and 1 tbsp oil. Coat everything well; even ten minutes of marinating helps, and an hour is better.

Spread on a lined sheet pan and roast at 230°C for 20 to 25 minutes, until the paneer is golden at the edges and the peppers are charred. Finish with cilantro and lemon. Serve with rice, naan or a big salad.
cards.example: Serves 2 at about 45 g protein each: roughly 65 g from the paneer, 20 g from the chickpeas and 10 g from the yogurt. Paneer is rich, so choose a lighter version or add extra chickpeas if you're watching calories.
cards.takeaway: A yogurt marinade and high heat make paneer a 45 g protein dinner.

cards.title: Meditations by Marcus Aurelius
cards.body:
Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire from 161 to 180 AD, through plague and near-constant war, and kept a private notebook he never meant to publish. Those notes to himself became Meditations, one of the most widely read works of practical philosophy.

It's Stoicism in action, drawing on Epictetus, whom Marcus admired: reminders to focus on what's in his control, to treat others fairly even when they disappoint him, to remember that fame and pain are both brief. Reading it feels less like a lecture and more like overhearing a powerful person trying to stay decent.

Translation matters a lot. Gregory Hays's 2002 version is modern and readable. Don't go cover to cover; read a few entries each morning.
cards.example: Start with Book 2, entry 1, where he prepares each morning to meet people who will be meddling, ungrateful and arrogant, and resolves not to be harmed or angered by them. Then read Book 1, his list of what he learned from the people in his life.
cards.takeaway: Read a few entries each morning; it's a manual for staying steady.

cards.title: The Italian Game: an opening to own
cards.body:
After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4, you're in the Italian Game, one of the oldest openings in chess and still popular at every level, including the very top. White develops quickly, aims the bishop at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp because only the king defends it, and prepares to castle.

The classical line, the Giuoco Piano, continues 3...Bc5 4.c3, planning d4 to build a big pawn centre. Modern players often prefer a slower setup with d3, building up patiently before striking.

The Italian rewards principles over memorization: develop knights before bishops, castle early, fight for the centre, and don't move the same piece twice without a reason. Learn the ideas and you'll handle most replies.
cards.example: Watch for the trap 3...Nd4 after 3.Bc4. Grabbing the pawn with 4.Nxe5? runs into 4...Qg5!, hitting the knight and g2 at once, and White is suddenly in serious trouble. Calmly castling or playing 4.c3 is better.
cards.takeaway: Develop, castle, aim at f7, and fight for the centre.

cards.title: Margin of safety: room to be wrong
cards.body:
Benjamin Graham, Buffett's teacher, called margin of safety the central concept of investment in the final chapter of The Intelligent Investor. The idea: since your estimate of a business's value is uncertain, only buy when the price sits well below it.

The gap protects you from your own mistakes, bad luck and events nobody could foresee. If you think a stock is worth $50 and buy at $49, any error hurts you. Buy at $33 and you can be quite wrong and still do fine.

In practice, margin of safety comes from more than price: conservative assumptions, strong balance sheets, and businesses whose value doesn't hinge on one rosy forecast. It also explains why great investors pass on most ideas. Waiting for the right price is part of the job.
cards.example: Your DCF says intrinsic value is $50 a share. With a one-third margin of safety, your buy price is about $33. If your cash flow forecasts prove 20% too optimistic, true value is closer to $40, and you still profit.
cards.takeaway: Buy at a big discount to value so being wrong doesn't ruin you.

quiz.question: What does it mean when the yield curve is inverted?
options: Long-term yields are far above short-term yields
Short-term yields are above long-term yields
Bond prices are rising across all maturities
quiz.explanation: Inversion means short rates exceed long rates, usually because markets expect future rate cuts and slower growth.

quiz.question: You run 40 km a week. Using the 20–30% guideline, about how long should your long run be?
quiz.explanation: 20 to 30 percent of 40 km is 8 to 12 km, so about 10 km fits.

quiz.question: What gives the paneer golden, charred edges in the sheet-pan tikka?
options: Marinating it overnight in lemon juice only
quiz.explanation: High oven heat browns the yogurt marinade and paneer quickly without drying it out.

quiz.question: In the Italian Game, why does White's bishop on c4 target f7?
options: It's where Black's queen usually goes
It's the only square the bishop can reach
Early in the game only Black's king defends it
quiz.explanation: f7 is guarded only by the king at the start, which makes it Black's weakest point.

quiz.question: You estimate intrinsic value at $80 a share and want a 25% margin of safety. What is your maximum buy price?
Review: Under the Taylor rule, if inflation rises 1 point above target and the output gap is unchanged, how should the policy rate move?
quiz.explanation: Inflation enters once directly and again at half weight through the gap term: 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 points. From Friday's Taylor rule card.
